questions.stem: A historian asks why a table of land totals shows a sharp fall in acres held jointly by members of a tribe after 1887. Explain in your own words how a change of title produced that fall.

answer.exemplar: Before 1887 the land of the tribe was held in common, so each family used overlapping tracts and no family held a separable share of the estate. The allotment act broke that common estate into surveyed parcels and issued patents to individual heads of families, so the figure for jointly held acreage fell sharply even though no acre of the reservation was destroyed.

questions.explanation: The exemplar must tie the fall in joint acreage to a change of title rather than a loss of land. Common and patented parcels can cover the same ground.

answer.exemplar: The statute authorised the President to designate a district to which particular tribes, or parts of tribes, could be removed, to cause the removal to be carried out, and to provide for the subsistence of those removed during the journey. options.misconception: Places notification after the gathering at the agency

options.text: Parents notified, children gathered at the agency, escort provided, transport, then classes.
Army escort provided, transport to the school, parents notified, children assembled, enrolment in classes.
options.misconception: Puts the transport before the army escort

options.text: Parents notified, children gathered, transport to the school, escort provided, then classes.
options.misconception: Puts transport before the escort was provided

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Where the power to deal with the tribes was placed
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a hearing record shows the commission doing

stimulus.body: From the hearing record of the division commission: 'The Commission has examined the application of the applicant for a place on the roll, has taken testimony as to the date of his removal to this country, and finds the application to be in accordance with the law. The applicant is hereby admitted as a citizen of the tribe and is entitled to select a parcel of land.'

questions.stem: The record above shows the commission doing which of the following?

options.text: Recording a treaty promise of annuity payments in exchange for tribal land.
options.misconception: Reads a roll hearing as an annuity negotiation

options.text: Exchanging land for a promise of loyalty to the United States government.
options.misconception: Reads the hearing as a loyalty bargain

options.text: Admitting a person to the roll on evidence of residence, with the entitlement to select land.
Suspending the tribal government until the land had been surveyed.
options.misconception: Reads a single hearing as a suspension of government

questions.explanation: The record shows the commission taking testimony on residence and admitting the applicant to the roll with the right to select land. A loyalty bargain is not described.
questions.hint: Weigh each option against the wording of the record.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a removal statute authorised
questions.learningObjective: Identify the conditions a removal statute placed before a removal

stimulus.body: Extract from a removal statute: 'No tribe or part of a tribe shall be removed from the country in which it now resides until the district intended for its reception has been selected, the country surveyed, and the necessary funds appropriated for the expense of the removal.' A further section provided for the chiefs who conducted the move.

questions.stem: The extract above places conditions before a removal. Which reading is correct?

options.text: No conditions applied, because the President could act by proclamation on his own signature.
options.misconception: Denies the conditions the extract states

options.text: Tibes could be removed at once, and the destination chosen afterwards to suit the settlers.
options.misconception: Reverses the order of designation and removal

options.text: Only the appropriation was required; the district could be chosen by the travellers themselves.
options.misconception: Reduces the conditions to the funding alone

options.text: A designation of the destination district, a survey and an appropriation had to precede the removal.

questions.explanation: The statute withheld removal until a district was selected, the country surveyed and the money appropriated, so three steps came first. Removing first contradicts the words.
questions.hint: Count the steps the extract lists before removal.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The allotment that replaced a land held in common
questions.learningObjective: Combine patent records with a land office summary
questions.stem: A patent table and a land office summary are read together. The patents name individual allottees; the summary lists parcels withdrawn for public use. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The patents show the whole estate stayed tribal, because patents were issued to the tribe as a body.
options.misconception: Treats patents to individuals as patents to the tribe

options.text: Land passed to individual owners by patent, while some tracts were withdrawn for schools and public purposes.
The tracts for public use were taken from the allotments of individual citizens without payment.
options.misconception: Invents an uncompensated taking from individual allottees

options.text: The summary proves that no patent was valid, because the land office doubted the roll.
options.misconception: Claims the land office repudiated the patents

questions.explanation: Patents to named individuals alongside tracts taken for schools show individual ownership and public withdrawals from one estate. Treating the patents as tribal goes beyond the sources.
questions.hint: Let both documents describe what happened to the land.

questions.topic: Who the statute counted as a head of family
questions.learningObjective: Apply the statutory acreage to a table of roll categories
questions.stem: A roll table gives applicants as 5,600 heads of family, 2,300 single persons over twenty-one, and 900 orphans over sixteen. Stage one, state the acreage each head of family received; stage two, compute the acreage going to heads of family.

options.text: Each head of family received 160 acres, so 5,600 heads of family account for 89,600 acres.
options.misconception: Drops a zero when multiplying

options.text: Each head of family received 80 acres, so 5,600 heads of family account for 448,000 acres.
options.misconception: Uses the smaller single-person figure for family heads

options.text: Each head of family received 160 acres, so 5,600 heads of family account for 896,000 acres.
Each head of family received 320 acres, so 5,600 heads of family account for 1,792,000 acres.
options.misconception: Doubles the statutory allotment without basis

questions.explanation: The statutory allotment for a head of family was 160 acres, and 5,600 times 160 gives 896,000 acres. Using the smaller single-person figure does not fit.
questions.hint: Multiply the head-of-family count by the statutory acreage.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: A school built to move a child away from a family
questions.learningObjective: Identify the stated aim of the school as its founders described it
questions.stem: A school table lists what students were taught and what they were forbidden to do. Which statement best describes the school's purpose as its founders saw it?

options.text: To return children to their families after a short course of reading and arithmetic.
options.misconception: Makes the school a brief course rather than a system

options.text: To preserve tribal society by recording the customs and languages of the children who attended.
options.misconception: Contradicts the school's stated aim of replacement

options.text: To produce a small cadre of literate clerks who would serve the reservation offices.
options.misconception: Reduces the school's aim to training clerks

options.text: To remake the children into American workers by replacing their language, religion and family life.

questions.explanation: Industrial training with rules against the pupils' language and religion shows an aim of remaking children into American workers. Sending them home after a short course contradicts it.
questions.hint: Read the forbidden practices as evidence of the aim.

questions.topic: Where the power to deal with the tribes was placed
questions.learningObjective: Compute total service years recorded in a commission report table
questions.stem: A commission report table lists officials and the years of their service: three served four years, five served three years, and two served two years. What was the total number of service years recorded?

options.text: 27 service years were recorded, leaving out the officials who served two years.
options.misconception: Omits a row of the table when totalling

options.text: 31 service years were recorded across the three groups of officials.
39 service years were recorded, adding the head count to the total.
options.misconception: Adds the number of officials to the service years

options.text: 22 service years were recorded, counting officials rather than years.
options.misconception: Counts the officials instead of the years served

questions.explanation: Three officials at four years, five at three and two at two give 12 plus 15 plus 4, which is 31 service years. Counting people rather than years misreads the column.
questions.hint: Multiply each group by its years, then add.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a removal statute authorised
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a removal act authorised and why the decision rested with officers
questions.stem: A statute table lists four powers granted by a removal act. Explain what the act authorised and why the decision to remove rested with federal officers.

answer.exemplar: The act authorised the President to select a district to which a named tribe or part of a tribe could be removed, to cause the removal to be carried out, and to provide for the subsistence of those removed during the journey. Because these powers were granted to the President and exercised by officers he appointed, the decision to remove and the conduct of the move rested with federal officers rather than with the tribal councils or with the states.

questions.explanation: The exemplar must name the designation, removal and subsistence powers and locate the decision in the President and his appointees. Stopping at the goal misses who acted.
questions.hint: Name the person the statute empowers, not only its purpose.

questions.learningObjective: Identify what happened to land released from tribal ownership
questions.stem: A land office table shows what happened to the land released from tribal ownership. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: It was opened to settlement by citizens of the United States under federal supervision.
It was granted to the states to be sold, with the proceeds divided among the families on the roll.
options.misconception: Claims the surplus was ceded to the states for sale

options.text: It was held in trust by the commission for members who had not yet selected their parcels.
options.misconception: Treats the surplus as reserved for later selection

options.text: It was divided among the schools, the churches and the civil authorities of the reservation.
options.misconception: Claims the surplus went to institutions

questions.explanation: The land released from tribal ownership was opened to settlement by citizens of the United States. Ceding it to the states or distributing it to institutions misstates the land office.
questions.hint: Ask who was allowed to take up the released land.

questions.topic: Who the statute counted as a head of family
questions.learningObjective: Sequence the steps by which a tribal roll was compiled and closed
questions.stem: A roll table lists the steps by which a tribal roll was compiled and finally closed. Which sequence is correct?

options.text: Applications received, names entered, the roll closed by Congress, residence and family verified.
options.misconception: Closes the roll before the verification is finished

options.text: Names entered on the roll, applications received, residence verified, and the roll closed by Act of Congress.
options.misconception: Puts the recording of names before the applications

options.text: Applications received, residence and family verified, names entered, and the roll closed by Congress.
Residence and family verified, the roll closed by Congress, applications received, names entered.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: A school built to move a child away from a family
questions.learningObjective: Identify what happened to graduates from a training school

stimulus.body: From the record of the school's first graduating class: 'The boys who leave us are placed with employers who agree to give them wages, food and clothing, and who promise to send them to church when they are idle. We keep a register of every boy we send out, and we visit them once a year.' The class numbered twenty-three boys.

questions.stem: The record above shows what happened to pupils after they left the school. Which reading is correct?

options.text: Pupils were paid a yearly allowance by the government until each reached the age of twenty-one.
options.misconception: Invents a government allowance for the graduates

options.text: Pupils returned to their families, where the school checked on their progress by letter.
options.misconception: Puts the pupils at home rather than with employers

options.text: Pupils were sent directly into the army, where the school visited their companies once a year.
options.misconception: Sends the graduates into the army instead of to employers

options.text: Pupils were placed with employers and supervised by the school through a register and an annual visit.

questions.explanation: The record says graduates were placed with employers while the school kept a register and visited them annually. Sending them home departs from the record.
questions.hint: Note who employed the graduates and who followed them.
